sections.overview: The blue acara is a freshwater cichlid native to northern South America and Trinidad, with populations in the Orinoco, Maracaibo, and upper Magdalena drainages.
sections.identification: It has an oval, moderately compressed body, usually olive to grey-blue, with faint dark bars and fine iridescent blue-green lines on the cheek. Males tend to be larger and more colourful than females, with brighter blue tones during breeding. FishBase records a maximum total length of 16 cm for male or unsexed fish; no reliable adult mass, body width, or body height was found in the consulted species references.
sections.habitat: It occurs in clear or turbid rivers, from still pools to flowing reaches, and also uses shallow streams, swamps, and floodplains.
sections.diet: It is an opportunistic omnivore. A Colombian stomach-content study found plant remains, fish, detritus, and insects; fish were consumed most during low or rising water, while plant material dominated at high or falling water.
sections.behavior: Breeding pairs become territorial around their nest and both parents guard the eggs and young.
sections.reproduction: The pair excavates a nest in sand or mud and guards its brood. Maturity is reported at about 9.5 cm total length, and multiple partial spawns may occur over a prolonged breeding season.
sections.ecology: The accepted name is Andinoacara pulcher; Aequidens pulcher is an older synonym. The related tree entry Aequidens diadema belongs to the same cichlid tribe, Cichlasomatini, but is a distinct species in a different genus.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment lists it as Least Concern and suspects a stable population trend because the species persists in modified waters. The total population size is unknown, and habitat quality continues to decline in parts of its range.
